ABSTRACT
The evolution of modern power systems into smart grids is increasingly powered by Artificial Intelligence (AI) 
and Machine Learning (ML), which provide effective solutions for managing renewable intermittency, dynamic 
demand, and cybersecurity challenges. This paper presents a comprehensive review of AI/ML applications in 
smart grids, tracing their development from foundational paradigms to cutting-edge technologies such as 
Federated Learning (FL), Generative AI (GenAI), Large Language Models (LLMs), the Artificial Intelligence of 
Things (AIoT), and Digital Twin (DT)-driven intelligence. Enabling infrastructures, including IoT, 5G, edge–cloud 
ecosystems, and ML-based smart sensors, are discussed alongside advanced approaches such as multi-agent 
systems. Key applications explored include load forecasting, predictive maintenance, anomaly and cyber- 
attack detection, demand-side management, and electric vehicle integration. Special emphasis is placed on 
Digital Twin and LLM architectures, which enable real-time cyber-physical replicas and context-aware reasoning, 
thus improving predictive analytics, resilience, and autonomous decision-making. Despite notable advance-
ments, challenges remain in interoperability, data privacy, computational scalability, adversarial robustness, and 
ethical constraints. By synthesizing these insights, the study highlights the transformative role of AI in creating 
resilient, sustainable, and intelligent energy systems, and outlines future research trajectories toward stan-
dardized DT frameworks, active learning paradigms, and LLM-driven energy intelligence.
Introduction
The global economy continues its growth trajectory with an ever- 
increasing reliance on energy consumption. However, the widespread 
utilization of fossil energy poses a severe threat to the environment, 
unequivocally highlighting the urgent need for a global transition to-
wards large-scale clean energy generation and utilization[1].In response 
to these pressing environmental challenges and escalating energy de-
mands, novel concepts in energy and electric power system development 
have emerged, focusing on the establishment of smart grids (SGs) and 
advanced power systems. These sophisticated networks aim to create a 
dynamic and intelligent interconnection among all energy participants, 
including generation sources, transmission and distribution networks, 
consumers, and even electric vehicles [2]. Over recent decades, elec-
trical power systems have undergone a profound evolution, trans-
forming from traditional, centralized structures into advanced next- 
generation smart grids. Early power grids, primarily designed for 
unidirectional power delivery from large, centralized power plants to 
consumers, faced inherent limitations in terms of efficiency, reliability, 
and scalability [1].These passive architectures lacked the capability to 
effectively manage the fluctuations introduced by intermittent renew-
able energy sources (IRES) and non-linear consumption patterns, often 
leading to power mismatches and even blackouts. As time progressed, 
the grid evolved into a decentralized and dynamic system, significantly 
enhancing flexibility, security, and efficiency through two-way power 
and information flow. These advancements have paved the way for a 
smarter, more resilient, and sustainable energy infrastructure [3].
At the heart of this transformative shift lies Artificial Intelligence (AI) 
and Machine Learning (ML). These technologies offer innovative solu-
tions to address the complexities of modern power systems and the 
challenges associated with integrating intermittent renewable energy 
sources and managing dynamic demand. By enabling real-time data 
analysis, predictive maintenance, demand-response optimization, and 
automated fault detection, AI plays a fundamental role in augmenting

The Internet of Things (IoT) is one of the promising technologies that 
can improve the operation and administration of smart grids. IoT de-
vices are linked to resources that are physically situated elsewhere and 
carry out their responsibilities by exchanging energy and data without 
the need for human involvement. Data-driven control systems and IoT 
technologies generate a network of smart factories, houses, smart cities, 
and smart grids. Under IoT-based networks, the efficiency of trans-

For instance, this research [5] developed a SCADA-controlled smart

remote monitoring and appliance control through TCP/IP and MQTT 
protocols. Their system prioritizes energy efficiency, user comfort

intelligent energy management. This work complements the broader

Smart meters detect energy usage in real-time, interact with the

two-way communication. The new power generation stations include 
many distributed generation (DG) technologies, such as photovoltaic

power grid as a result of this paradigm change from the traditional grid 
to the smart grid. As such, the smart grid will integrate new smart 
technologies into distributed and renewable generation systems to make 
the traditional power grid more productive, efficient, and intelligent [6].

ment. These include the timely transmission of critical operational

human-dependent analysis and decision-making, transforming conven-

gent infrastructures. By leveraging powerful computational resources, 
advanced learning models, and massive data, AI ensures secure, reliable, 
economical, and environmentally sustainable operation of next-

Abstract
Day-ahead dispatch of integrated energy systems (IESs) is commonly solved by mixed-
integer linear programming when objectives, constraints, and forecasts are fully specified.
In practice, however, operators often express temporary preferences in natural language,
and day-ahead forecasts inevitably deviate from realized operation. These two conditions
make a fixed optimization interface difficult to use without additional modeling effort.
This paper proposes DARC (Decompose-Act-Repair-Critique), a constraint-diagnostic LLM
agent framework for day-ahead dispatch of campus-level microgrid-type IES with under-
specified operating requirements. DARC combines three language modules, namely a
Decomposer for temporal structure, a Resolver for numerical schedule generation, and a
Critic for root-cause diagnosis, with deterministic repair, constraint checking, and metric
evaluation. In all main experiments, the Decomposer is instantiated by its determinis-
tic rule-based variant for reproducibility, so the reported results reflect a loop with two
LLM modules (Resolver and Critic). The Projector repairs candidate schedules where
possible, while the Checker supplies mathematical facts that ground the Critic’s feedback.
DARC does not model forecast uncertainty through sets or scenarios; robustness to forecast
deviation is pursued operationally, through margin-aware repair and checker-grounded
revision, and is assessed empirically. Experiments on a campus-level microgrid IES testbed
show that DARC can incorporate natural-language preferences, improve realized feasibility
under forecast noise relative to both a point-forecast MILP and an interval-robust MILP
baseline in terms of strictly feasible configurations, at higher operating cost, and produce
diagnostic feedback that is robustly more useful than an ungrounded LLM diagnoser under
judge models from three families, and at least as useful as checker facts alone, with its ad-
vantage concentrated in actionable revision guidance. DARC is therefore positioned not as
a replacement for MILP , robust formulations, or model predictive control on fully specified
problems, but as a complementary interface for operational settings where preferences and
forecasts are not completely formalized.

1. Introduction
As low-carbon transition and campus energy digitalization continue to advance,
distributed photovoltaics (PV), battery storage, combined heat and power (CHP) units,
and electrified heating devices are increasingly coordinated through unified energy-
management platforms. Energy hubs and multi-carrier optimal power flow provide early
modeling foundations for integrated energy systems (IESs) [1,2]. Mancarella [3] reviewed
multi-energy-system concepts and evaluation models, while Mohammadi et al. [4] summa-
rized the development of the energy-hub model. Compared with single-carrier electricity
dispatch, day-ahead IES dispatch must simultaneously coordinate grid transactions, bat-
tery charging and discharging, CHP operation, electric boilers, and thermal storage. Its
difficulty arises from the joint effects of electricity–heat coupling, inter-temporal storage
dynamics, and device-level safety limits.
When objectives, constraints, and exogenous forecasts are fully formalized, MILP and
MPC remain mainstream and verifiable tools for IES dispatch. Zhang et al. [5] reviewed
modeling and solution methods for integrated electricity–heat operation, and Wu et al. [6]
proposed a multi-time-scale economic MPC framework that responds to forecast updates
and state changes through rolling optimization. Constrained MPC has a mature theoretical
basis [7] and has been applied to microgrid and risk-aware operation problems [8,9]. This
paper therefore does not position LLMs as replacements for MILP or MPC on fully specified
mathematical models. Instead, it focuses on operational information that is not yet fully
formalized but still affects dispatch decisions.
Such under-formalized information commonly appears in two forms. The first is
operator preference. Requirements such as maintenance windows, asset-life management,
low-carbon operation, or peak-period output suppression are often expressed in natural
language during operation. They can be translated after the fact into inequalities, soft
objectives, or counting constraints, but this process requires manual modeling and is
difficult to scale to changing operational expressions. The second is forecast deviation.
Day-ahead load and PV forecasts inevitably differ from realized profiles, and a schedule
optimized for point forecasts may violate power balance, state-of-charge (SOC) bounds,
or terminal conditions on the execution day. Robust optimization characterizes the trade-
off between conservativeness and economic performance [10], and has been used in IES
planning and hybrid AC/DC microgrid energy management [ 11,12]. However, these
methods usually require uncertainty to be represented as sets, intervals, distributions, or
risk measures, and cannot directly process temporary operating preferences expressed in
free text.
LLMs provide a possible bridge between natural-language requirements and struc-
tured decision workflows. Retrieval-augmented generation enables language models to
use external memory [ 13], while ReAct and Toolformer show that LLMs can combine
language reasoning with external actions or tool calls [ 14,15]. In the energy domain,
Majumder et al. [ 16] discussed the capabilities and limitations of LLMs in the electric-
energy sector; Antonesi et al. [17] and Zhang et al. [18] further reviewed opportunities and
reliability challenges for LLM-enabled energy systems. Existing applications include inter-
pretable building control [19], optimization with unstructured building-energy data [20],
distribution-system state estimation [21], and virtual-power-plant analysis [22]. However,
day-ahead dispatch differs from question answering, explanation, or state recognition. It
requires 24 h numerical schedules that satisfy electricity–heat balance, device capacities,
SOC dynamics, and terminal constraints at every time step. If LLMs are introduced into
IES dispatch, their outputs must therefore be coupled with deterministic repair, constraint
checking, and feedback grounded in mathematical facts.

The shift to renewable power sources and building electrification to decarbonize existing
and emerging building stock present unique challenges for the power grid. Building loads
and flexible resources e.g. batteries must be adequately managed simultaneously to unlock
the full flexibility potential and reduce costs for all stakeholders. Simple control algorithms
based on expert knowledge e.g. rule-based control (RBC), as well as, advanced control

ABSTRACT
Building Energy Management Systems (BEMS) collect and monitor building operational data for energy effi-
ciency but face challenges such as complex data management, reliability issues, and a lack of holistic approaches 
to energy efficiency. To address these limitations, this study proposes Digital Twin-enabled BEMS (DT-BEMS), 
integrating Digital Twin technology with BEMS to enhance functionality. DT-BEMS uses the Brick schema to 
create a BEMS ontology and incorporates a virtual building model defined as a mathematical representation of 
building physical behavior. This model includes three behavioral models: the energy imputation model, the 
Predicted Mean Vote (PMV) virtual model, and the occupancy model. Holistic Operational Signature (HOS) 
analyzes building operation data, identifying patterns and relationships for comprehensive efficiency evaluation. 
In DT-BEMS, a rule-based HOS classifier enables real-time operational signature identification, generating energy 
efficiency insights. The process of energy efficiency information generation was continuously updated 
throughout the building operation stages to ensure reliability and accuracy. The proposed system was validated 
using one month’s data from an office space, with data expanded at three-day intervals. DT-BEMS identified 
eight operational signature types, achieving a 97.9 % accuracy rate when using just 12 days of data compared to 
a full month. During the study, 23.5 % of operations were identified as inefficient, with energy waste during 
unoccupied periods being the most prevalent (19.9 %). The virtual model improved identification accuracy by 
4.6 % of the data. Real-time operational signature identification was implemented in the Dynamo environment, 
highlighting DT-BEMS as a practical tool for enhancing building energy management, reducing inefficiencies, 
and supporting sustainable building operations.

1. Introduction
In the face of the growing importance of addressing the climate crisis 
and achieving carbon neutrality, building energy management has 
emerged as a crucial task for a sustainable future. Approximately 40 % of 
global energy consumption occurs in buildings, accounting for a sig-
nificant portion of total carbon emissions [1]. Urbanization and eco-
nomic growth have led to a continuous increase in building energy 
consumption, making efficient energy management a necessity rather 
than a choice [2]. Therefore, improving the energy efficiency of build-
ings is essential for reducing carbon emissions and mitigating climate 
change [3]. By effectively implementing energy management strategies, 
it is possible to lower energy consumption, reduce greenhouse gas 
emissions, and ultimately achieve sustainable development objectives.
Building Energy Management Systems (BEMS) are important tools 
used to monitor and control energy consumption within buildings, 
thereby enhancing energy efficiency [4]. BEMS collect real-time data 
through sensors and metering devices, analyze energy usage patterns, 
and propose optimized energy management strategies [5]. These sys-
tems integrate various building systems such as heating, cooling, light-
ing, and ventilation to maximize energy-saving effects. As a result, they 
reduce energy consumption, lower operational costs, and improve 
occupant comfort, making BEMS an essential component of modern 
building management. Furthermore, the information on building energy 
behavior and efficiency analyzed through BEMS during the building 
operation phase can significantly contribute to policy and certification 
systems, urban management, and the advancement of zero-energy 
building design and engineering in the construction industry [6]. This 
comprehensive data supports the development of informed energy pol-
icies, helps cities manage their energy resources more efficiently, and 
drives the construction industry towards achieving higher standards of 
sustainability [7].
However, traditional BEMS have several limitations. Primarily 
relying on sensor and metering-based monitoring incurs high installa-
tion and maintenance costs. The complexity of managing large volumes 
of data from various sensors can be challenging, and any issues with data 
accuracy and reliability can compromise the effectiveness of energy 
management. Additionally, these systems are often limited to data-based 
analysis, restricting the application of advanced energy efficiency so-
lutions [8]. There is also an insufficient understanding of the interaction 
between building physical behavior and energy consumption, which 
limits the potential for maximizing energy management effectiveness. 
To address these issues, a more sophisticated and integrated approach is 
necessary. By leveraging Digital Twin technology, which has been 
actively studied in recent years, the capabilities of BEMS can be 
enhanced [9]. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional 
BEMS, enabling more efficient building management.
The concept of the Digital Twin was first introduced at University of 
Michigan presentation in 2002 aimed at establishing a Product Lifecycle 
Management (PLM) center [10]. Digital Twin, initially proposed in the 
manufacturing industry, has continuously developed and is utilized 
across various industries for purposes such as monitoring, simulation, 
optimization, and diagnosis, among others [11]. Recently, a plenty of 
papers on Digital Twin have been published in the Architecture, Engi-
neering and Construction (AEC) industry [12]. Similar to its use in 
product lifecycle management in manufacturing, Digital Twin enables 
effective building management throughout the building lifecycle in 
construction. In particular, the focus of Digital Twin is on O&M (Oper-
ation and Maintenance) stage, where Digital Twin significantly con-
tributes to the operation and management of physical buildings [13].
Digital Twin technology creates a virtual model of physical systems, 
enabling real-time monitoring and prediction based on real-time data 
[10]. Tao et al. [11] proposed a five-dimensional Digital Twin concept, 
defined by physical entities, virtual models, services, and the connec-
tions between them.These connections, or relations, encompass the ex-
change of data, information, and knowledge. By applying Digital Twin 
technology to BEMS, interaction between the physical building and the 
virtual model, based on real-time data, becomes possible. From this 
perspective, integrating Digital Twin with BEMS provides energy effi-
ciency information or knowledge that reflects the building’s physical 
behavior using real-time data. Therefore, combining Digital Twin 
technology with BEMS can help address certain limitations, such as an 
overreliance on data-based analysis and a lack of comprehensive un-
derstanding of the building’s physical behavior and energy 
consumption.
Some studies have demonstrated the potential for integrating Digital 
Twin technology with BEMS. Faham et al. [14] explored the application 
potential of Digital Twin technology in building energy management, 
highlighting its ability to monitor, optimize, and predict energy con-
sumption in real time, thus contributing to sustainable building energy 
management and cost reduction. Moreover, Grieves and Vickers [10] 
have extensively discussed the potential of Digital Twins in enhancing 
the predictability and optimization of complex systems, which is 
applicable to building energy management as well. Zakharchenko and 
Stepanets [15] proposed the concept of Digital Twin as an integrated 
platform for Building Management Systems (BMS), Building Information 
Modeling (BIM), and Internet of Things (IoT) in building automation to 
enhance energy efficiency. Hwang et al. [16] proposed a Digital 
Twin-based BEMS (DT-BEMS), discovering a potential energy savings of 
17.2 % based on data from the past month. These studies underscore the 
potential of Digital Twin technology to enhance the accuracy and 
effectiveness of energy management systems. Applying Digital Twin 
technology to building energy management allows for more accurate 
energy management through real-time interaction between physical 
buildings and virtual models. This enables the implementation of 
advanced applications and significantly improves energy efficiency. 
Digital Twins can detect system changes and anomalies in real-time, 
allowing for immediate response, and contributing to long-term en-
ergy savings and cost reductions.
Despite the potential of integrating Digital Twin technology with 
BEMS, the technical development for embedding DT into BEMS remains 
insufficient, necessitating further studies [17]. The limitations of pre-

● Absence of a detailed methodology for virtual modeling: Exist-

improvement processes for virtual models during the O&M stage.

accommodate the variability inherent in building operations [18].

Digital Twin (DT) technologies are rapidly transforming the design, operation, and lifecycle management of 
renewable energy systems. This systematic review investigates DT applications across four major renewable 
energy domains—solar, wind, hydro, and hybrid systems—encompassing all lifecycle phases from initial design

global sustainability frameworks such as the UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and the EU Green Deal.

demic understanding, supports industrial innovation, and informs policy development for the next generation of

1. Introduction
1.1. Background and motivation
According to a recent white paper by the International Renewable 
Energy Agency (IRENA, 2022), digital technologies—including Digital 
Twins (DTs)—are central to enabling renewable energy scalability, 
flexibility, and real-time operational intelligence. The report un-
derscores the need for harmonizing digital innovation with policy, 
infrastructure, and regulation, emphasizing the importance of DTs in 
bridging physical infrastructure with digital capabilities across solar, 
wind, and hybrid systems. This digital transition is framed as a foun-
dational enabler for achieving the targets of the Paris Agreement and UN 
SDGs. In the last few decades, the energy sector has undergone a major 
transformation. This is because there is a necessity to address climate 
change, decrease reliance on fossil fuels, and protect the environment 
[1] discussed climate-related energy policies [2], focused on fossil fuel 
dependency, and [3] emphasized environmental sustainability. The 
goals of sustainability, structural resilience, and low-carbon emissions 
have brought the development of renewable energy technologies to the 
forefront of domestic and global policy frameworks. This shift is also a 
result of growing awareness about the risks posed by greenhouse gas 
emissions, the finite reserves of fossil fuels, the degradation of energy 
security due to geopolitical turmoil, and tensions in the fossil fuel-driven 
economy [4] noted geopolitical influences on energy security, while [5] 
elaborated on fossil fuel-driven economic tensions. In reaction, gov-
ernments, industries, and research organizations worldwide have step-
ped up their activities to harness renewable energy sources and integrate 
them into the current and future power infrastructure. Solar photovol-
taic (PV) and wind energy, as well as hydroelectric power, biomass, and 
geothermal energy, are now recognized as critical components for 
achieving global decarbonization targets. These clean and sustainable 
energy sources provide environmental protection by mitigating carbon 
emissions and pollution while also enhancing economic prosperity 
through long-term energy cost savings, diversification, and new 
employment opportunities. According to the International Energy 
Agency (IEA), by the end of this decade, renewables are projected to 
have over 90 % share in new installations of power capacity, making it 
the most predominant energy sector [6]. This growth also increases the 
importance of renewable sources in fulfilling global electricity re-
quirements as well as fulfilling climate targets such as the ones put 
forward in the Paris Agreement.
Even with their promise, renewable energy systems are deep rooted 
complicated and provide many operational and technological diffi-
culties. One of the more important issues is their strong dependency on 
environmental factors which are highly unpredictable and dynamic. The 
amplitude of solar irradiance, wind speed, ambient temperature, and 
humidity levels fluctuate remarkably over time and space which directly 
impact the energy output, achieving system performance stability and 
optimization becomes very difficult [7,8]. This variability brings a high 
level of risk, increasing the needs of sophisticated prediction, moni-
toring, control mechanisms, and reliability for ensuring grid stability. In 
addition, the growing decentralization and interconnection of renew-
able energy infrastructures through smart grids and distributed energy 
resources (DERs) adds new elements of complexity to system manage-
ment [9]. Oftentimes, traditional control and supervisory approaches 
are inadequate to address the changes within operational timeframes 
and fail to adequately represent the nonlinear interactions between the 
different components of the system. Therefore, advanced digital tech-
nologies are needed that would increase system observability, renew-
ables controllability, adaptability, and responsiveness to changing 
conditions [10]. Hence, digitalization stands as a primary driver, 
providing an array of tools and methods that can change how energy 
systems are imagined, designed, operated, and maintained. Among 
these technologies, DT appears as a particularly promising innovation. A 
DT is defined as a real-time digital counterpart of a tangible system that 
perpetually replicates its state, behavior, and performance [11]. In 
combination with data analytics, AI, and real-time sensors, DTs offer 
unrivaled visibility and insight into the operations of renewable energy 
assets [12]. The use of DT technologies in the renewable energy industry 
signifies a paradigm shift in how stakeholders manage uncertainty, 
failure prediction, and performance optimization. The ability of DTs to 
simulate operational environments, predict system deterioration, 
determine maintenance schedules, and respond to shifting parameters is 
unmatched. DTs enable the real-time application of intelligence and 
predictive controls with high precision and adaptability, resulting in 
enhanced system reliability, operational efficiency, and reduced costs 
[13]. With the continuing digital transformation of the worldwide en-
ergy sector, incorporating DTs into renewable energy systems will be 
crucial in building a resilient, intelligent, and sustainable energy future.
1.2. Definition and concept of DT
A Digital Twin (DT) is a recent technological innovation that enables 
real-time monitoring, analysis, and control of physical systems. It is a 
virtual representation of a physical asset, process, or system, continu-
ously updated based on live data from the physical counterpart. Unlike 
static simulations, DTs dynamically evolve with changes in system 
behavior, environmental conditions, and operational parameters [14]. 
This bi-directional, real-time integration enhances responsiveness across 
the asset’s lifecycle. DTs aggregate diverse data streams—including 
sensor readings, control signals, logs, and physics- or data-driven mod-
els—to closely replicate system performance [15]. This allows the DT to 
simulate scenarios, evaluate performance, diagnose faults, and support 
decision-making in near real-time [16]. The architecture typically 
comprises three layers: the physical system, digital model, and a data 
stream layer linking the two [17]. This framework applies to systems 
such as solar PV arrays, wind turbines, and hydroelectric generators. The 
digital layer incorporates design models, algorithms, and simulations, 
while the data stream layer ensures real-time feedback between the 
physical and virtual entities. Advanced DTs increasingly integrate AI, 
machine learning, and cloud or edge computing to enhance adaptability 
and intelligence [18]. AI supports anomaly detection and predictive 
maintenance, cloud computing manages large-scale data, and edge 
computing enables low-latency control. Collectively, these features 
make DTs core components of cyber-physical systems (CPS) for real-time 
optimization and autonomous control [19,20]. In renewable energy, 
DTs simulate solar panel performance under varying irradiance, tem-
perature, and shading conditions [21,22], and model wind turbine dy-
namics using real wind data and vibration profiles [23]. Hydropower 
DTs can emulate water flow and sediment accumulation to optimize 
output and maintenance. As renewable systems grow in complexity and 
data intensity, DTs are increasingly essential for enhancing efficiency,

From systematic evidence to agentic architectures: A systematic review and 
framework for large language model–driven smart grids
Zahra Rezaei , Mohammad Amin Amini , Yaser Mike Banad *
Gallogly College of Engineering, University of Oklahoma, Norman, OK, 73019, USA
HIGHLIGHTS
• A PRISMA review synthesizes 61 studies on AI and LLMs in smart grids.
• A three-level taxonomy defines LLM roles as interface, reasoner, and agent.
• A six-layer architecture unifies perception, reasoning, action, and governance.
• Digital twins and engineering tools enable verified, bounded grid autonomy.
• Key barriers include reliability, latency, cybersecurity, safety, and regulation.
ARTICLE INFO
Keywords:
Large language models
Agentic artificial intelligence
Cyber-physical energy systems
Digital twins
Multi-agent coordination
Trustworthy smart grids
ABSTRACT
Modern smart grids increasingly rely on intelligent decision-support systems to coordinate distributed energy 
resources, renewable generation, and complex cyber–physical infrastructures. Although recent advances in 
artificial intelligence (AI) have substantially improved forecasting, optimization, and operational analytics, 
existing solutions remain largely fragmented, with limited system-level integration of perception, reasoning, 
coordination, and execution.
To address this gap, this study conducts a Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 
(PRISMA)-guided systematic review of 61 peer-reviewed papers published between 2019 and 2026. Based on the 
extracted evidence, an evidence-informed six-layer architectural framework is proposed that integrates physical 
data acquisition, semantic context abstraction, large language model reasoning, multi-agent coordination, tool- 
augmented execution, digital twin validation, and cross-layer governance into a unified smart grid intelligence 
architecture.
The review shows that recent research has progressively evolved from isolated predictive models toward 
cognitive and agent-based decision-support systems; however, no existing framework provides an integrated 
architecture that simultaneously combines semantic reasoning, engineering tool orchestration, digital twin 
verification, governance mechanisms, and human oversight. To bridge this gap, the proposed framework es-
tablishes a perception–reasoning–action workflow and is further illustrated through an operational use-case 
scenario demonstrating the interaction between heterogeneous data sources, specialized agents, engineering 
tools, validation mechanisms, and decision support.
The analysis indicates that large language models can significantly enhance contextual reasoning, coordina-
tion, explainability, and operational adaptability when deployed as cognitive orchestrators rather than auton-
omous controllers. Nevertheless, practical deployment remains constrained by challenges including numerical 
reliability, inference latency, cybersecurity, operational safety, and regulatory compliance, requiring bounded 
autonomy supported by engineering verification, digital twin simulation, governance policies, and human-in-the- 
loop supervision.
This work provides an evidence-informed architectural foundation for trustworthy next-generation smart grid 
intelligence and offers a structured roadmap for future research on integrating large language models into real- 
world energy system operation.

1. Introduction
The rapid evolution of modern power systems toward decentralized, 
data-intensive, and cyber-physical infrastructures has fundamentally 
reshaped smart grids. The integration of renewable energy, distributed 
energy resources (DERs), electric vehicles, and intelligent demand-side 
management has transformed smart grids into dynamic systems 
requiring real-time, uncertainty-aware decision-making. In this context, 
AI and machine learning (ML) have become key enablers of forecasting, 
optimization, and system resilience [1,2].
Over the past decade, AI-driven approaches have been widely 
applied in smart grids, including load forecasting, anomaly detection, 
demand response, and predictive maintenance. Deep learning models 
such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs), convolutional neural net-
works (CNNs), and reinforcement learning (RL) have demonstrated 
strong performance in modeling nonlinear spatio-temporal dynamics [3,
4]. More recently, paradigms such as federated learning (FL) and digital 
twins (DTs) have been introduced to address data privacy, scalability, 
and cyber-physical integration challenges [5,6]. However, most existing 
approaches remain task-specific and lack cross-domain reasoning and 
system-level coordination capabilities.
Recent comprehensive reviews have further emphasized that the 
transition toward renewable-dominated power systems introduces sig-
nificant planning and operational challenges, including distributed 
resource coordination, uncertainty management, multi-objective opti-
mization, and resilient microgrid operation. These challenges require 
integrated decision-support mechanisms capable of combining plan-
ning, optimization, and operational intelligence across multiple tem-
poral and spatial scales. Although existing reviews primarily focus on 
optimization algorithms and energy management strategies, they pro-
vide important context for understanding why more advanced cognitive 
architectures based on LLMs and agentic AI are emerging as comple-
mentary decision-support technologies for future smart grids [7].
In parallel, large language models (LLMs), enabled by transformer- 
based architectures [8], have introduced new capabilities in contex-
tual reasoning, planning, and cross-task generalization. Foundation 
models such as GPT-style architectures have demonstrated strong per-
formance in multi-step reasoning, tool utilization, and decision support 
with minimal task-specific training [9]. These capabilities position LLMs 
as promising candidates for bridging the gap between data-driven ana-
lytics and high-level decision intelligence in complex cyber-physical 
systems.
However, the application of LLMs in smart grids remains in its early 
stages. Existing studies primarily employ LLMs as natural language in-
terfaces for querying data, generating reports, or supporting operator 
interaction, rather than as integral components of decision-making 
pipelines [10]. This limited perspective underutilizes their potential as 
cognitive engines capable of orchestrating heterogeneous models and 
coordinating distributed energy systems.
A key limitation of current smart grid intelligence is the absence of a 
unified architectural framework that integrates perception, reasoning, 
and action. Existing ML pipelines typically operate in isolation, opti-
mizing individual tasks without capturing system-level interactions. As 
smart grids evolve into decentralized and multi-agent environments, 
there is a growing need for holistic, context-aware intelligence that 
enables coordinated and adaptive decision-making across heteroge-
neous components.
Recent advances in agentic AI and tool-augmented LLMs introduce a 
new paradigm in which systems can decompose tasks, invoke external 
tools, and iteratively refine decisions through feedback loops [11,12]. 
This paradigm enables LLMs to function not merely as predictive 
models, but as orchestrators of multi-step decision processes across 
interconnected subsystems.
To address this gap, this study introduces a structured taxonomy of 
LLM roles in smart grids across three functional levels: interface, 
reasoner, and agent. These roles capture the progression from natural 
language interaction to context-aware reasoning and, ultimately, to 
autonomous coordination and tool-augmented decision-making.
Building on this taxonomy, the paper proposes a six-layer architec-
ture for LLM-driven smart grids, in which LLMs function as central 
reasoning and orchestration components within a cyber-physical sys-
tem. The framework integrates data acquisition, context abstraction, 
LLM-based reasoning, multi-agent coordination, tool-augmented 
execution, and cross-layer governance, enabling a coherent percep-
tion–reasoning–action pipeline. In this design, LLMs transform raw grid 
data into structured representations, generate context-aware decisions, 
and coordinate domain-specific tools such as forecasting and optimiza-
tion models. Integration with digital twins further supports closed-loop 
feedback, allowing decisions to be simulated and refined prior to 
deployment.
Methodologically, the study adopts a dual approach combining 
PRISMA-guided systematic review with conceptual architectural syn-
thesis. A total of 61 papers are analyzed to identify recurring patterns, 
capability gaps, and emerging design principles in LLM-enabled smart 
grid intelligence. The resulting contributions include: (i) a systematic 
evidence synthesis of LLM and AI applications in smart grids; (ii) a 
domain-specific taxonomy of LLM roles; (iii) an evidence-informed 
architectural framework; and (iv) a structured analysis of key chal-
lenges, including scalability, safety, latency, and trustworthiness.
Importantly, the proposed taxonomy and architecture are not pre-
sented as direct outputs of individual studies, but as higher-order con-
ceptual syntheses derived from structured evidence aggregation. 
Accordingly, the architecture should be interpreted as a design-oriented 
abstraction that organizes fragmented literature into a coherent system- 
level perspective, rather than as a fully validated end-to-end 
implementation.
This work does not introduce a new standalone algorithm, but pro-
vides the first domain-specific integration of LLM role taxonomy with 
cyber-physical smart grid architectures, bridging semantic reasoning, 
agentic coordination, and energy system constraints.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 pre-
sents the research methodology. Section 3 introduces the taxonomy of 
LLM roles. Section 4 describes the proposed architecture. Section 5
provides the thematic synthesis of the reviewed papers. Section 6 dis-
cusses challenges and future directions. Section 7 presents the limita-
tions of the study. Section 8 concludes the paper.
2. Methodology
This study was designed as a systematic literature review aimed at 
identifying, screening, and synthesizing the body of research related to 
artificial intelligence, machine learning, and more specifically LLM- 
driven intelligence in smart grids. In addition to summarizing prior 
studies, the review was structured to support the development of a 
conceptual taxonomy and a multi-layer architectural framework for 
LLM-driven autonomous smart grids. Accordingly, the methodology 
combined a PRISMA-guided screening process with structured evidence 
extraction and thematic synthesis.
The review protocol was designed to answer three interrelated 
research questions: 
(1) How have AI- and ML-based approaches evolved in smart grid 
research toward LLM-enabled intelligence?
(2) What functional roles are currently assigned to LLMs in energy 
systems, and where are the major conceptual and practical gaps?
(3) What architectural patterns, enabling technologies, and unre-
solved challenges can inform the design of autonomous, agentic, 
and trustworthy smart grid systems?
To address these questions, the review followed a stepwise pipeline 
involving search strategy design, eligibility definition, PRISMA-based 
study selection, and structured data extraction.

ABSTRACT
As residential energy systems become increasingly electrified and coordination-intensive, home energy man-
agement systems (HEMS) must operate economically while remaining aligned with evolving user-authorized 
comfort and service boundaries. Existing personalization approaches rely on questionnaire initialization, fixed 
preference parameters, or indirect behavioral corrections, limiting alignment under changing needs and the use 
of runtime natural-language feedback for long-horizon calibration. This paper proposes a large language model 
(LLM)-enabled human-in-the-loop framework that converts user utterances into authorization-aware, contract- 
constrained, machine-checkable events for downstream control and preference updating. The LLM is a contract- 
constrained semantic interface, not a direct controller. Explicit intents support bounded execution and direct 
profile correction, whereas vague feedback requires option negotiation and user confirmation before bounded 
updating. A Contract-Informed Preference Update (CIPU) mechanism combines structured interaction evidence 
with projection and trust-region stabilization, while model predictive control remains the safety-constrained 
execution layer. In simulations, the proposed method reduces normalized preference distance by 22.50% and 
complaints by 74.46% relative to Survey MPC across three role-conditioned profiles. On a controlled 188-utter-
ance language-interface benchmark, the proposed interface achieves 100% structured-event exact match and a 
0% parser-level false direct-execution rate. Closed-loop ablations show 59.40% fewer complaints than the 
explicit-only variant, while event-log auditing of the no-contract-gate variant yields a 36.90% event-interface 
mismatch rate after gate removal. Under mid-horizon preference drift, final preference mismatch is reduced 
by 44.09% on average and up to 71.43% relative to Survey MPC.

1. Introduction
1.1. Background and motivation
As end-use electrification deepens, the operational complexity of the 
energy transition is increasingly shifting from the traditional supply side 
to end-use energy systems. The IEA reports in Electricity 2026 that 
global electricity demand grew by about 3% year-on-year in 2025 and is 
projected to increase by around 3.6% per year on average during 
2026–2030 [1]. In parallel, Energy Efficiency 2025 reports that build-
ings account for roughly 30% of global energy demand, with residential 
buildings contributing about 70% of building energy use [2]. Under this 
trend, homes are evolving into small multi-device energy systems in 
which critical loads such as HVAC and electric vehicle (EV) charging 
must be continuously coordinated under time-varying prices, weather 
conditions, and user routines. U.S. EIA residential end-use statistics 
further show that space cooling and space heating remain among the 
major household electricity end uses [3]. Accordingly, home energy 
management systems (HEMS) can no longer be viewed as static sched-
uling tools. Their practical effectiveness increasingly depends on 
whether automated control decisions can remain aligned with residents' 
evolving comfort, service, and cost-related requirements during sus-
tained operation.
A fundamental challenge is that the controllability of critical residential 
loads is not determined by device physics alone. It is more appropriately 
understood as user-conditioned operational flexibility, jointly shaped by 
comfort tolerance, temporary tasks, behavioral preferences, and willing-
ness to accept control actions. Consequently, system-level coordination 
demand does not automatically translate into callable household control 
authority. Stable coordinability can be preserved only if HEMS can 
continuously perceive, confirm, and maintain user-authorized controllable 
boundaries over time. This makes sustained user alignment not an auxiliary 
feature, but a core requirement for practical residential energy coordina-
tion. The urgency of this requirement is reinforced by the fact that, ac-
cording to the IEA's Global Energy Review 2025, electricity use in buildings 
increased by more than 600 TWh in 2024, accounting for nearly 60% of the 
global electricity-demand increment that year, with air-conditioning 
growth as an important driver [2].
In real home settings, however, such boundaries are often context- 
dependent, evolving, and difficult to express through fixed parameters 
alone. Users may need to communicate immediate requests, nuanced 
comfort corrections, or gradual shifts in operating preference, and these 
signals are naturally expressed in language rather than in predefined nu-
merical forms. Prior work has demonstrated the feasibility of natural- 
language interfaces in related cyber-physical and IoT settings [4]. This 
makes natural language a practical and low-friction channel for conveying 
high-level user intent, but it also creates a critical interface mismatch: user 
utterances are semantically rich yet unstructured, whereas downstream 
control and optimization require consistent, machine-checkable inputs. 
Moreover, runtime language feedback often mixes different control se-
mantics, including directly executable instructions and longer-horizon 
preference evidence. Without a robust interface that can separate and 
stabilize these signals, short-term expressions may interfere with long-term 
preference calibration, weakening sustained alignment between control 
actions and user needs. A central question for modern HEMS is therefore 
how natural-language feedback can be transformed into stable, verifiable, 
and reusable evidence for both real-time execution and long-horizon 
preference updating.
1.2. Related work and motivation for this study
Existing HEMS personalization studies have mainly incorporated user 
needs in two ways. One line parameterizes user needs through comfort 
ranges, preference weights, or control-related settings and then embeds 
these quantities into scheduling or optimization models. For example, Liu 
et al. developed a data-driven, uncertainty-aware preference modeling 
pipeline and incorporated the identified preference levels into multi- 
objective HEMS scheduling [5], while Ren et al. combined comfort eval-
uation with reinforcement learning-based decision making to address 
control under uncertain household parameters [6]. Another line adapts 
preferences during operation using indirect feedback signals, such as 
thermostat overrides or online behavioral traces. Elehwany et al. learned 
preferences from thermostat override behavior [7], and Sha et al. contin-
uously updated control-relevant models through online learning [8]. 
Taken together, these studies have moved HEMS from one-shot setup to-
ward dynamic adaptation. However, by representing user needs primarily 
as preset parameters or by inferring them indirectly from sparse behavioral 
evidence, they remain limited by a relatively low-bandwidth feedback 
loop. As a result, they are not well suited to absorb semantically rich run-
time language feedback as explicit, reusable evidence for sustained closed- 
loop calibration.
To make such semantically rich runtime feedback usable by HEMS, 
the system must first identify the user's intent and determine whether 
the utterance should trigger control-related processing. Wu et al. 
developed SCADA-NLI, which combines hierarchical intent classifica-
tion with semantic parsing to translate natural-language queries and 
control instructions into structured intermediate commands, achieving 
96.5% intent-recognition accuracy and 88.47% instruction-parsing ac-
curacy [9]. Larson et al. constructed an evaluation dataset covering 150 
intents across 10 domains and showed that benchmark classifiers per-
formed well on supported intents but struggled to identify out-of-scope 
queries [10]. These studies show that conventional intent recognition 
and scripted parsing pipelines can effectively map language into 
machine-readable representations when task classes and semantic 
boundaries are specified in advance. In sustained HEMS operation, 
however, the same temperature or SOC value may denote a requested 
target, a current measurement, a historical record, or a candidate option, 
while some utterances express only an adjustment direction and others 
contain no current control request. Covering these cases with predefined 
rules or fixed intent labels requires the relevant expressions and se-
mantic roles to be specified beforehand, limiting their ability to process 
open-form runtime feedback.
To interpret such open-form expressions, large language models 
(LLMs) have opened new possibilities for natural-language interaction in 
building and energy systems. In building operation and maintenance, Li 
et al. mapped natural-language queries to database access and question- 
answering responses using LLM-based methods [11], while Chen et al. 
developed a domain-adapted large-model framework for building en-
ergy system O&M with integrated domain knowledge [12]. At a broader 
methodological level, LLMs have also been explored for building load 
forecasting [13] and for more general building energy management 
tasks [14]. Human-in-the-loop mechanisms have likewise been explored 
through user confirmation, overrides, and feedback correction in 
building- and control-related settings. However, while LLMs are effec-
tive for query assistance, advisory support, and local interaction, a 
fundamental tension remains between the non-deterministic, open- 
ended nature of language generation and the strict feasibility re-
quirements of constraint-based control. This tension becomes especially 
important when moving from read-oriented assistance to closed-loop 
control participation. In such settings, unconstrained language outputs 
cannot be directly treated as executable control signals. What is still 
missing is a constrained intermediate representation that can transform 
mixed-semantic runtime feedback into stable, verifiable, and reusable 
evidence for both real-time execution and long-horizon preference 
calibration. This unresolved interface problem directly motivates the 
contract-constrained framework developed in this paper.

Based on the above review, we identify three key research gaps.

The residential sector has received great attention worldwide due to its significant contribution to energy con­
sumption and carbon emissions. Although Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) based Home Energy Management 
(HEM) has provided promising solutions for user comfort satisfaction and energy savings, existing approaches 
still face three challenges: (1) accurately perceiving dynamic user preferences, (2) efficient learning with limited 
data samples, and (3) protecting user privacy during data sharing. To address these issues, a Large Language 
Model (LLM)-enhanced HEM with dynamic user preference elicitation and hierarchical data-sharing is proposed, 
introducing three key innovations. First, the Knowledge-Guided Chain-of-Thought method is proposed to per­
ceive dynamic user preferences from unconstrained natural language interactions, by leveraging users’ historical 
knowledge as explicit guidance. Second, the LLM-generated reference actions based on shared knowledge and 
preference descriptions are proposed to accelerate the learning process under conditions of cold-start situations.

enable effective knowledge inference from natural language while preserving user privacy. Simulation results in 
the household scenario with dynamic user preferences demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves sig­
nificant improvements in both user preference elicitation and learning efficiency, ultimately leading to a 28.8% 
reduction in cost and a 9.3% improvement in comfort compared to fixed preference DRL methods.

The continuous growth in global energy consumption needs has in­
tensified environmental pollution and climate change, leading to a shift 
toward greener energy systems. The residential energy sector is a crit­
ical area for low-carbon transitions [ 1] due to its high proportion of 
total energy consumption, and its energy demand is still rising. In 2019, 
residential electricity consumption accounted for 26.6% of total elec­
tricity consumption [ 2]. The Home Energy Management (HEM) plays 
a crucial role in enhancing home energy efficiency by optimizing en­
ergy usage, improving reliability, and integrating renewable energy 
sources [3,4].

Current approaches to HEM primarily fall into two paradigms: 
model-based and data-driven. Model-based energy management meth­
ods reduce total energy costs by modelling and controlling the energy 
usage of a house while meeting the comfort requirements of occu­
pants [5–7]. A typical model-based method is Model Predictive Control 
(MPC) [8], which first predicts model parameters and then optimizes 
control actions using a mathematical solver. To integrate the PV-battery, 
the scenario-based stochastic MPC is applied  [ 9]. Also, adaptive ro­
bust MPC is utilized by introducing an additional uncertainty model to 
represent load disturbances  [10]. Moreover, reference [11] introduced 
MPC through Monte Carlo uncertainty quantification and vehicle-to-
home communication protocols. Although model-based methods offer 
a promising solution for HEM, these methods rely on precise modelling 
and struggle to adapt to dynamic preferences, which prevents achieving 
optimal performance of HEM in the high uncertainty environment.
Data-driven approaches have transformed HEM by eliminating mod­
elling dependencies while enhancing adaptability [ 12]. Reinforcement 
Learning (RL) is the typical method that can minimize home energy 
cost in a dynamic environment [ 13,14]. An important research direc­
tion of RL-based HEM is to consider the application in a more complex 
environment, such as extending to multi-energy coordination  [ 15,16], 
considering real-time demand response for optimal scheduling of home 
appliances  [ 17,18], and dealing with the uncertainty of electricity 
prices [19]. Also, the learning efficiency and performance are improved 
through reward shaping  [ 20] and combining a knowledge-driven 
model [21]. Recently, the new attempt is to incorporate the personal­
ized preferences in the HEM process, such as customers’ and operators’ 
perspectives  [ 22], and residents’ feedback and activity [ 23]. Despite 
the significant improvements in the approaches, existing data-driven 
methods still face two major challenges. First, difficulty in accurately 
perceiving users’ dynamic numerical preferences, or preference elicita­
tion, through a human-friendly, unconstrained natural language dialog. 
Second, the low learning efficiency and performance occur under condi­
tions of limited data samples, especially when the environment and user 
preferences change.
Recent advancements in Large Language Model (LLM) have demon­
strated strong capabilities in natural language understanding, reasoning, 
and judgment [24,25]. On one hand, LLMs have emerged as a promis­
ing approach to augment RL, referred to as LLM-enhanced RL, improving 
multitask learning, sample efficiency, and high-level task planning [26]. 
The Action-Guider paradigm of LLM-enhanced RL demonstrates how 
LLMs improve learning efficiency through two key mechanisms. First, 
for large action spaces, such as text-based games, LLMs directly gen­
erate high-value action candidates [ 27,28]. Second, LLMs improve the 
quality of policy-generated actions by utilizing inherent expert knowl­
edge [29,30]. On the other hand, for the HEM, the natural language 
understanding and reasoning capabilities of LLMs enable precise user 
preference elicitation through unconstrained natural language. This, in 
turn, assists RL agents in formulating a more accurate reward func­
tion and addresses the traditional difficulty of modelling personalized 
preferences in RL-based HEM.
Building on these insights, an innovative LLM-enhanced HEM frame­
work with dynamic user preference elicitation and a hierarchical 
data-sharing mechanism is proposed, which introduces four major con­
tributions:
1. Innovative LLM-Enhanced HEM Framework: A novel control 
framework that synergistically integrates LLM, RL, and a data-
sharing mechanism is proposed to address the core challenges of 
dynamic user preference elicitation, efficient learning, and privacy 
protection in RL-based HEM.
2. Dynamic User Preference Elicitation: To accurately perceive dy­
namic user preferences through unconstrained natural language 
interaction, the Knowledge-Guided Chain-of-Thought (KG-CoT) 
reasoning is proposed by leveraging users’ historical knowledge 
as explicit guidance and incorporating a reflection mechanism, 
enabling the accurate capture of hourly comfort and objective 
numerical changes in users.
3. LLM-enhanced Action Guidance: To mitigate cold-start explo­
ration risks in home energy systems, the LLM-enhanced action 
guidance mechanism which leverages relevant knowledge from 
similar users is proposed. By transferring such cross-user knowl­
edge, the mechanism accelerates RL learning under limited data 
samples and improves energy management performance in envi­
ronments with dynamic user preferences.
4. Hierarchical Data-Sharing Mechanism: A hierarchical data-sharing 
mechanism integrated with LLM-based knowledge extraction is 
proposed to enable effective knowledge inference from uncon­
strained natural language while preserving user privacy, which 
facilitates efficient and targeted data selection for downstream 
learning and decision-making.
The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. An overview of 
the HEM model is introduced in Section 2. Then, a detailed method­
ology of our proposed framework is presented in Section 3. Section 4 
demonstrates the framework’s control performance through comprehen­
sive simulation results. Section 5 concludes with key findings and future 
research directions.
2 . Home energy management modelling
HEM needs to monitor and control energy generation, storage, and 
consumption within a household. HEM usually optimizes for a goal 
such as cost reduction, self-sufficiency maximization, or emissions mini­
mization. With the increasing adoption of electric mobility and heating, 
residential PV, and dynamic tariffs, HEM is gaining popularity as the sav­
ings potential increases. The models normally include renewable energy 
generation, battery energy storage, and heat transfer.
Fig. 1 illustrates the modular architecture of the HEM system. The 
core of the system is the HEM Controller, which is responsible for mak­
ing intelligent energy management decisions. It perceives the current 
environmental state by collecting information from both indoor (e.g., 
indoor temperature, power usage) and the external system (e.g., outdoor 
temperature, real-time electricity prices). Based on this information, the 
controller sends control signals to the physical components within the 
home environment, including the renewable energy generation, energy 
storage, and controllable loads. The ultimate goal of this control process 
is to optimize a set of predefined long-term objectives, namely energy 
cost, carbon emissions, and user comfort. The detailed mathematical 
models for the key components within the environment are presented 
in the following subsections.

ABSTRACTS
Intelligent detection and diagnosis methods have shown great potential in identifying faults of building energy 
systems. However, practical applications remain limited due to its reliance on prompt engineering, the developed 
models, and a lack of interpretability. To address these challenges, this study develops an agentic fault detection 
and diagnosis (AFDD) framework that integrates the AI agent, ontology, and generalized diagnosis rules. The 
ontology can describe the knowledge of buildings and control logic. The generalized diagnosis rules can diagnose 
the fault of the actuator, sensor, load, plant in other control loops, and setpoint. And the AI agent combined with 
ontology and diagnosis rules generates interpretable diagnosis reports and suggestions. The AFDD framework is 
validated on a real-world heating, ventilation, and air conditioning (HVAC) system. The result shows that the 
framework achieves information extraction for building energy system and supply air temperature control loop 
and realizes ontology extension for the supply chilled water temperature. All faults for the supply air sensor, 
temperature control valve, cooling capacity, supply chilled water temperature and unreasonable setpoint can be 
automatically diagnosed without misjudgment using data form one hour, one day, to one week. The diagnosis 
report including the fault number, breakdown, and detailed analysis and operation and maintenance suggestions 
are generated. In summary, the AFDD framework enhances automation, interpretability, and decision-making for 
building energy systems. It provides a new perspective for the next-generation intelligent diagnosis method.
1. Introduction
As one of the most resource-intensive sectors, the building industry is 
responsible for approximately 40 % of global primary energy con-
sumption and over 30 % of total carbon emissions. This offers consid-
erable potential for energy conservation and carbon reduction [1,2]. 
Building energy systems are an essential part of large public buildings, 
which consume significant energy [3,4]. In recent years, the rapid 
advancement of sensor, communication, computing, and control tech-
nologies has positioned automatic control as one of the effective stra-
tegies for optimizing energy efficiency [5]. Through the real-time 
monitoring and intelligent adjustment of operational parameters, 
automatic control systems can decrease energy consumption while 
increasing indoor environmental comfort [6]. At present, widely 
implemented automatic control strategies encompass open-loop control 
[7], closed-loop control [8], proportional–integral–derivative (PID) 
control [9], and model predictive control [10,11]. Automatic control 
enhances system stability and responsiveness compared to traditional 
manual operation or simple time-based scheduling. It facilitates dy-
namic optimization in response to fluctuating loads, changing climatic 
conditions, and varying user demands, further advancing overall energy 
performance.
However, the practical implementation of automatic control strate-
gies continues to face several challenges, including sensor failures, 
actuator stuck, higher load, unreasonable setpoint, and negative influ-
ence from other control loops [12–14]. For instance, Li et al. [15] 
discovered that adjusting the temperature control valve resulted in the 
control fault when the error of the supply air temperature was +2 ◦C, at 
which the control loop of the PID reached a stable time lag exceeding 
20.6 % . Similarly, Verhelst et al. [16] reported that faults in tempera-
ture sensors may induce economic losses in control performance ranging 
from 7 % to 1000 %. Consequently, fault detection and diagnosis (FDD) 
for control loops has become increasingly important in building energy

systems [17–19]. By monitoring and analyzing operational conditions, 
FDD facilitates the timely identification and localization of potential 
faults. This prevents abnormal increases in energy consumption and 
enhances system stability.
Many researchers have proposed different FDD approaches for 
building energy systems and control loops to facilitate automatic fault 
identification, isolation, and maintenance. The FDD approaches can be 
classified into three categories: model-based approaches [20,21], 
data-driven approaches [22,23], and knowledge-based approaches [24,
25]. Model-driven approaches are used to develop mathematical models 
that characterize the system’s behavior. Based on these models, residual 
sequences are generated and analyzed against predetermined thresholds 
to identify fault conditions. The effectiveness of this approach is closely 
tied to the accuracy of the system model, necessitating a certain level of 
domain expertise for practical implementation. With the development of 
the big data technology, data-driven approaches have attracted more 
and more attention. Data-driven approaches rely on many operational 
data and employ data mining techniques to analyze system performance 
for fault diagnosis, including principal component analysis, support 
vector machines, neural networks, and deep learning. While data-driven 
approaches provide significant advantages in terms of detection and 
ease of implementation, their performance is largely dependent on the 
accuracy and quality of data collected from system sensors and equip-
ment. Moreover, knowledge-driven approaches leverage causal models, 
detailed system descriptions, or expert knowledge to construct diagnosis 
rules for fault detection. These approaches do not depend on the quality 
of measurement and can be highly effective; however, they often require 
a substantial accumulation of expert knowledge, which can be both 
time-consuming and labor-intensive.
Recently, with the ongoing refinement of intelligent building oper-
ation and maintenance standards by international organizations such as 
ASHRAE, alongside the adoption of cutting-edge technologies, an arti-
ficial intelligence (AI) agent driven FDD approach has provided new 
ways for intelligent diagnostics and adaptive operation of various sys-
tems [26–28]. The AI agent is powered by large language models (LLMs) 
such as Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) by OpenAI and 
Gemini by Google [29]. It has demonstrated the ability to comprehend 
complex concepts, engage in sophisticated reasoning, and integrate in-
formation across multiple domains [30–32]. LLMs in the fault diagnosis 
industry possess domain knowledge like domain experts, enabling them 
to diagnose faults and anomalies based on users’ prompts and analyze 
data like domain experts [33]. For example, Lannger et al. [34] utilized 
the sequential processing capabilities of LLMs to handle time-series data 
from HVAC systems. And the models were further fine-tuned using many 
labeled input data to achieve binary or multiclass fault classification. 
Zhang et al. [35] applied GPT to diagnose common faults in AHUs, 
chillers, and variable refrigerant flow air conditioners. They could 
provide interpretable texts explaining the reason behind their diagnosis 
results. To further enhance diagnosis accuracy, Zhang et al. [36] 
designed a self-correction strategy for LLMs that automatically generates 
an optimized training dataset based on labeled data to improve the 
LLM’s performance. Additionally, a data augmentation method was 
proposed to adapt and optimize the training dataset, enabling iterative 
development of high-performance LLMs. Moreover, Li et al. [28] diag-
nosed the fault of the virtual model of return temperature of chilled 
water in building digital twins based on 10 consecutive residuals greater 
than the threshold.
These approaches have propelled the progress and advancement of 
FDD. However, when applied to real-world building energy systems, 
several limitations need to be considered: 
(1) Existing FDD approaches relied on user prompt to provide 
building information and control logic, which increased the time 
and cost required for system deployment and development.
(2) System-specific knowledge or black-box models were employed 
to achieve FDD for the sensor or equipment. However, the control 
loop including the sensor, actuator, load, setpoint, and plant was 
neglected, which reduces the performance of operation and 
maintenance.
(3) Previous FDD methods focused on diagnosis effect using various 
evaluation indexes, decision-making processes behind responses 
were not interpretable.
Hence, this study develops an agentic fault detection and diagnosis 
(AFDD) framework that combines the ontology, generalized FDD rules, 
and the AI agent, achieving advancements in automated cross-scenario 
generalizability, result interpretability, and practical decision support 
capability. This work presents a novel solution for efficiently operating 
and maintaining building energy systems and promoting energy con-
servation and carbon reduction. Moreover, the effectiveness of the AFDD 
framework in the real building energy system has been further validated 
through the discussion of the running time and field experiments.
The main contributions of this study are as follows: 
(1) Ontology is developed by leveraging the Brick schema and its 
extensions for control logic to describe the knowledge of building 
energy systems and control loops to reduce the required time and 
cost for providing this information.
(2) Generalized FDD rules are proposed based on by incorporating 
operational and maintenance experience, design instructions, 
expert knowledge, and historical data to diagnose the sensor, 
actuator, load, setpoint, and plant in real building energy systems 
with high accuracy and applicability, which achieves manage-
ment of key equipment and points.

ABSTRACT  
Faults, such as malfunctioning sensors, equipment, and control systems, significantly affect a building’s per-
formance. Automatic fault detection and diagnosis (AFDD) tools have shown great potential in improving 
building performances, including both energy efficiency and indoor environment quality. Since modern buildings 
have integrated systems where multiple subsystems and equipment are coupled, many faults in a building are 
cross-level faults, i.e., faults occurring in one component that trigger operational abnormalities in other sub-
systems. Compared with non-cross-level faults, it is more challenging to isolate the root cause of a cross-level 
faults due to the system coupling effects. Bayesian networks (BNs) have been studied for the root cause isola-
tion for building faults. While promising, existing BN-based diagnosis methods highly rely on expert domain 
knowledge, which is time-consuming and labor expensive, especially for cross-level faults. To address this 
challenge, we propose an entropy-based causality learning framework, termed Eigen-Entropy Causal Learning 
(EECL), to learn BN structures. The proposed method is data-driven without the use of expert domain knowledge; 
it utilizes causal inference to determine the causal mechanisms between faults status and symptoms to construct 
the BN model. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, three fault test cases are used for 
evaluation in this study. Experimental results show that the BN constructed by the proposed framework is able to 
conduct building cross-level faults diagnosis with a comparable isolation accuracy to those by domain knowledge 
while maintaining less complexed BN structure.   
1. Introduction 
Building Heating, Ventilation and Air conditioning (HVAC) systems 
are complex with a variety of sensors, subsystems and automatically 
controlled components. According to the United Nations Environment 
Programme, approximately 135 EJ operational energy demand and 10 
Gt energy-related carbon dioxide emission were attributed to the 
building systems in 2021 [1]. It is also reported that 30 % of this energy 
usage [2] was wasted due to malfunctioning sensors and components in 
the HVAC systems [3,4]. Automatic fault detection and diagnosis 
(AFDD) technologies thus are vital to ensure satisfactory building per-
formances, especially from the aspect of energy efficiency [5]. Field 
studies and practices indicate that AFDD technologies cannot only 
achieve up to 20 % building energy savings [6,7] but also improve 
equipment lifecycles and indoor comforts [8–10]. 
Modern building HVAC systems typically include a set of multiple, 
highly coupled subsystems such as cooling/heating plant, primary air 
distribution, and terminal air distribution subsystems. Due to the 
coupling effect among building components, a fault occurring in one 
equipment or subsystem may propagate and influence other equipment 
or subsystems [11,12]. Hence, component-level AFDD methods may not 
be efficient and suitable solutions to the root cause analysis for cross- 
level faults, i.e., faults causing adverse effects across multiple compo-
nents and subsystems [13]. Chen et al. [13] has provided an example of 
a chiller supply water temperature sensor bias fault (e.g., sensor reading 
higher than actual temperature) in the chiller plant which would cause 
the cooling valve open position in a downstream air handling unit

tool that only monitors the AHU might result in false alarms such as a

root cause analysis is necessary to ensure the correct diagnosis of cross-
